claim: The locus coeruleus (LC) houses the vast majority of noradrenergic neurons in the brain.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC) houses the vast majority of noradrenergic neurons in the brain and regulates many fundamental functions, including fight and flight response, attention control, and sleep/wake cycles.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by extensive prior research.

claim: The LC regulates fight and flight response, attention control, and sleep/wake cycles.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC) houses the vast majority of noradrenergic neurons in the brain and regulates many fundamental functions, including fight and flight response, attention control, and sleep/wake cycles.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about LC function.

claim: LC noradrenergic neurons are diverse and could be classified into two major morpho-electric types.
source: LC noradrenergic neurons are diverse and could be classified into two major morpho-electric types.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from morphological and electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fast excitatory synaptic transmission among LC noradrenergic neurons was not observed in the preparation.
source: While fast excitatory synaptic transmission among LC noradrenergic neurons was not observed in our preparation, these mature LC neurons connected via gap junction at a rate similar to their early developmental stage and comparable to other brain regions.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from testing more than 1500 cell pairs.

claim: Mature LC neurons connect via gap junctions at a rate similar to their early developmental stage.
source: While fast excitatory synaptic transmission among LC noradrenergic neurons was not observed in our preparation, these mature LC neurons connected via gap junction at a rate similar to their early developmental stage and comparable to other brain regions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing adult and juvenile mice.

claim: Most electrical connections form between dendrites.
source: Most electrical connections form between dendrites and are restricted to narrowly spaced pairs or small clusters of neurons of the same type.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of electrically coupled pairs.

claim: Electrical connections are restricted to narrowly spaced pairs or small clusters of neurons of the same type.
source: Most electrical connections form between dendrites and are restricted to narrowly spaced pairs or small clusters of neurons of the same type.
evidence: This is supported by connectivity analysis as a function of inter-soma distance and cell type.

claim: More than two electrically coupled cell pairs were often identified across a cohort of neurons from individual multicell recording sets that followed a chain-like organizational pattern.
source: In addition, more than two electrically coupled cell pairs were often identified across a cohort of neurons from individual multicell recording sets that followed a chain-like organizational pattern.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from multicell recordings and statistical modeling.

claim: The assembly of LC noradrenergic neurons follows a spatial and cell-type-specific wiring principle that may be imposed by a unique chain-like rule.
source: The assembly of LC noradrenergic neurons thus follows a spatial and cell-type-specific wiring principle that may be imposed by a unique chain-like rule.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and statistical modeling comparing observed patterns to random connectivity models.

claim: The LC sends widespread noradrenergic projections to all major divisions of the central nervous system (CNS).
source: The locus coeruleus (LC) is a small pontine nucleus that houses the vast majority of norepinephrine (NE)-producing neurons in the brain and sends widespread noradrenergic projections to all major divisions of the central nervous system (CNS) (Schwarz and Luo, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: LC dysregulation is implicated in various neuropsychiatric conditions, including depression, anxiety, autism spectrum disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder.
source: By releasing NE across the CNS, the LC participates in many cognitive processes and behaviors crucial for survival, including fight and flight response, attentional control, and sleep/wake cycles, while its dysregulation is implicated in various neuropsychiatric conditions, including depression, anxiety, autism spectrum disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder (Bast et al., 2018; Fortress et al., 2015; Southwick et al., 1999; Weinshenker, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: LC/NE neurons are heterogeneous in terms of anatomical projections, morpho-electric profiles, and specific behavioral functions.
source: However, increasing evidence supports LC/NE neurons are heterogeneous in terms of the anatomical projections, morpho-electric profiles, and specific behavioral functions they involve (Bari et al., 2020; Hirschberg et al., 2017; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The LC is composed of multiple specialized noradrenergic modules with nonoverlapping LC/NE neurons with specific electrophysiological properties and projection targets.
source: Particularly, recent tracing studies coupled with behavioral paradigms suggest that the LC is composed of multiple specialized noradrenergic modules. Each module comprises nonoverlapping LC/NE neurons with specific electrophysiological properties and projection targets, thus participating in distinct functions of the circuits within its efferent domain (Chandler et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016; Totah et al., 2019; Uematsu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LC/NE neurons within each module are able to switch from a discrete, patterned coding mode to a global broadcast mode to cope with more demanding situations.
source: Interestingly, LC/NE neurons within each module are also able to switch from a discrete, patterned coding mode to a global broadcast mode to cope with the more demanding situation (Uematsu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Monoamine neurons, including LC/NE neurons, could co-release glutamate to engage in fast neurotransmission.
source: Increasing evidence suggests monoamine neurons, including LC/NE neurons, could co-release glutamate to engage in fast neurotransmission as well (Fung et al., 1994a; Fung et al., 1994b; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NE can be released locally in the LC to activate α2 adrenoceptor (α2AR) on the same or adjacent LC/NE neurons to initiate a negative feedback mechanism regulating their excitability.
source: It appears that NE can be released locally in the LC to activate α2 adrenoceptor (α2AR) on the same or adjacent LC/NE neurons to initiate a negative feedback mechanism regulating their excitability (Aghajanian and VanderMaelen, 1982; Egan et al., 1983; Huang et al., 2007; Williams et al., 1985), but it remains to be illustrated whether these neurons can interact with each other via fast neurotransmission.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gap junctions among LC/NE neurons appear to be prevalent only in neonates and decline significantly with age.
source: However, gap junctions among LC/NE neurons appear to be prevalent only in neonates and decline significantly with age (Christie and Jelinek, 1993; Christie et al., 1989; Travagli et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Each brainstem slice prepared from adult mice with an NMDG-based slicing protocol contained numerous healthy LC neurons.
source: Each brainstem slice prepared from adult mice with an NMDG-based slicing protocol contained numerous healthy LC neurons (Jiang et al., 2015; Kuo et al., 2020; Ting et al., 2014), allowing for simultaneous patch-clamp recordings of up to eight mature LC neurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and references to the slicing protocol, with Figure 1A showing the recording setup.

claim: Simultaneous patch-clamp recordings of up to eight mature LC neurons were achieved.
source: Each brainstem slice prepared from adult mice with an NMDG-based slicing protocol contained numerous healthy LC neurons (Jiang et al., 2015; Kuo et al., 2020; Ting et al., 2014), allowing for simultaneous patch-clamp recordings of up to eight mature LC neurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LC/NE neurons at rest had a highly depolarized resting membrane potential (RMP, –43.0 ± 0.1 mV, n=289).
source: LC/NE neurons at rest had a highly depolarized resting membrane potential (RMP, –43.0 ± 0.1 mV, n=289), and all neurons were spontaneously active at rest (1.6 ± 0.4 Hz, n=30; Figure 1B), similar to previous reports on LC neurons (Andrzejewski et al., 2001; Ballantyne et al., 2004; Kuo et al., 2020), but different from hippocampal neurons (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements from 289 neurons, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All LC/NE neurons were spontaneously active at rest (1.6 ± 0.4 Hz, n=30).
source: LC/NE neurons at rest had a highly depolarized resting membrane potential (RMP, –43.0 ± 0.1 mV, n=289), and all neurons were spontaneously active at rest (1.6 ± 0.4 Hz, n=30; Figure 1B), similar to previous reports on LC neurons (Andrzejewski et al., 2001; Ballantyne et al., 2004; Kuo et al., 2020), but different from hippocampal neurons (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements from 30 neurons, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: LC/NE neurons were charged much more slowly with a higher input resistance compared to both types of hippocampal neurons in response to negative current injection.
source: In response to negative current injection, LC/NE neurons were charged much more slowly with a higher input resistance compared to both types of hippocampal neurons (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing LC neurons to hippocampal neurons, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The majority of LC/NE neurons exhibited a characteristic pause after their first action potentials (APs) followed by a series of APs in response to prolonged suprathreshold positive current injection.
source: In response to prolonged suprathreshold positive current injection, the majority of LC/NE neurons exhibited a characteristic pause after their first action potentials (APs) followed by a series of APs, which departed significantly from stereotypical firing patterns of hippocampal neurons (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: LC/NE neurons had much wider action potentials with a lower amplitude, followed by a deep and prolonged afterhyperpolarization compared to hippocampal neurons.
source: LC/NE neurons were also unique in their single APs, which were much wider with a lower amplitude, followed by a deep and prolonged afterhyperpolarization compared to hippocampal neurons (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing action potential properties, shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: t-SNE-based clustering approach clearly separated LC neurons from the two types of hippocampal neurons.
source: To illustrate strikingly distinct properties of LC/NE neurons, we extracted 13 electrophysiological features from three groups of neurons (see 'Materials and methods') and plotted them in a t-SNE-map. This t-SNE-based clustering approach clearly separated LC neurons from the two types of hippocampal neurons (Figure 1D), highlighting the unique electrophysiological properties of LC neurons.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of electrophysiological features, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Most LC neurons were large cells with smooth dendrites (aspiny), similar to CA1-PVs in the hippocampus, but different from CA1-PCs with spiny dendrites.
source: Most LC neurons were large cells with smooth dendrites (aspiny), similar to CA1-PVs in the hippocampus, but different from CA1-PCs with spiny dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: LC/NE neurons had more tortuous dendritic trees with less branch order than hippocampal neurons.
source: In addition, their dendritic trees were more tortuous with less branch order than hippocampal neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: LC/NE neurons could be grouped into two major types: fusiform cells (FF) and multipolar cells (MP).
source: LC/NE neurons had diverse somatodendritic shapes, based on which we could group them into two major types: fusiform cells (FF) and multipolar cells (MP) following previous nomenclature (Swanson, 1976).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis and supported by citation to prior nomenclature.

claim: FFs had an elongated, usually spindle-shaped large soma with two, or rarely three, primary dendrites originating from opposite poles of the soma.
source: FFs had an elongated, usually spindle-shaped large soma with two, or rarely three, primary dendrites originating from opposite poles of the soma (Figure 2C, D and F).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations shown in Figures 2C, D, and F.

claim: MP had a triangular or nearly round soma with more than three primary dendrites that could originate from any side of their soma.
source: The second type of neurons, MP, had a triangular or nearly round soma with more than three primary dendrites that could originate from any side of their soma (Figure 2A, B and F).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations shown in Figures 2A, B, and F.

claim: The dendrites of MPs branched more profusely around the soma compared to that of FF.
source: The dendrites of MPs also branched more profusely around the soma compared to that of FF (Figure 2A, B and G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figures 2A, B, G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Two types of neurons were well separated in a plot of soma bipolarity against bipolarity index of dendritic arborization.
source: To support LC neuron classification, we reconstructed a subset of LC/NE neurons and quantified their soma bipolarity (i.e., the ratio of the major to the minor axis of a fitted ellipse of the soma; the larger the ratio, the more bipolarity the soma exhibits) and the bipolarity index of dendritic arborization (the proportion of the dendrites originating around the major axis of the fitted ellipse; the larger the proportion, the more bipolarity the dendritic arborizations exhibits) (Figure 2E), and then plotted these two parameters against each other. Two types of neurons were well separated in this plot (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on quantitative morphological analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A nonlinear neural network-based classifier could separate two types with a performance accuracy of 100%.
source: We also trained a nonlinear neural network-based classifier to distinguish cell types and the classifier could separate two types with a performance accuracy of 100% (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is based on machine learning analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Soma shape is a reliable criterion to distinguish two types of neurons.
source: Of note, the performance using soma shape alone was almost as good as the performance using two parameters (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B), suggesting that soma shape is a reliable criterion to distinguish two types of neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from machine learning analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Most MPs had their axon originating from the soma (~80%, 37 out of 46 reconstructed MPs).
source: FFs generally had the axon originating from one of the primary dendrites (~95%, 37 out of 39 reconstructed FF neurons, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that most FFs have privileged dendrites (i.e., synapses made on these axon-bearing dendrites are in an electrotonically privileged position in evoking action potentials)(Häusser et al., 1995), while most MPs had their axon originating from the soma (~80%, 37 out of 46 reconstructed MPs; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations from 46 reconstructed MPs, shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MPs had less local axonal arborization as compared to FFs.
source: In addition, MPs had less local axonal arborization as compared to FFs (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The axon in many MPs had the first branching point located >400 µm away from their origin.
source: The axon in many MPs had the first branching point located >400 µm away from their origin, while the axon in FFs branched much earlier and formed denser local axonal arborization than MPs (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: FFs constitute ~38% of total LC/NE neurons (250 out of 666 recovered LC/NE neurons).
source: FFs and MPs had different population sizes (MP: ~62%, 416 out of 666 recovered LC/NE neurons; FF: ~38%, 250 out of 666 LC/NE neurons).
evidence: This is based on counting recovered neurons from the experimental dataset.

claim: MPs constitute ~62% of total LC/NE neurons (416 out of 666 recovered LC/NE neurons).
source: FFs and MPs had different population sizes (MP: ~62%, 416 out of 666 recovered LC/NE neurons; FF: ~38%, 250 out of 666 LC/NE neurons).
evidence: This is based on counting recovered neurons from the experimental dataset.

claim: FFs were not evenly distributed across the entire LC, but preferentially localized in certain anatomical positions.
source: Given that FFs constitute ~38% of total LC/NE neurons, the proportion of FFs in each multicell recording set (the cohort of >3 LCs neurons from each slice) should fall most frequently within the range of 30–40% if FFs are evenly distributed across the entire LC. However, this was not the case in the histogram of FF proportion (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) across all recording sets. Instead, the FF proportions were heavily biased toward either the range of 0–20% or of 50–100%, suggesting that FFs were not evenly distributed across the entire LC, but preferentially localized in certain anatomical positions.
evidence: This is inferred from statistical analysis of FF proportions across recording sets, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: FFs had a narrower spike with a larger amplitude than MPs.
source: FFs had a narrower spike with a larger amplitude than MPs (Figure 2I, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements comparing FF and MP, shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The spikes from FF and MP had different temporal dynamics.
source: The spikes from the two cell types also had different temporal dynamics (measured at the first spike evoked by our step protocol, Figure 2I, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 2I.

claim: FFs could be evoked more spikes with large suprathreshold depolarizing current injections than MPs.
source: In addition, FFs could be evoked more spikes with large suprathreshold depolarizing current injections than MPs (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: More than 1500 LC neuron pairs were tested for synaptic connections.
source: We tested more than 1500 LC neuron pairs, most of which have an inter-soma distance <150 µm (Figure 3C), but no single excitatory synaptic connection was detected (Figure 3D) despite prominent spontaneous EPSPs present in each potential postsynaptic neuron.
evidence: This is based on experimental testing of cell pairs, shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: No single excitatory synaptic connection was detected among tested LC neuron pairs.
source: We tested more than 1500 LC neuron pairs, most of which have an inter-soma distance <150 µm (Figure 3C), but no single excitatory synaptic connection was detected (Figure 3D) despite prominent spontaneous EPSPs present in each potential postsynaptic neuron.
evidence: This is based on experimental testing of more than 1500 cell pairs, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: No visible hyperpolarization in potential postsynaptic cells following single presynaptic APs or a train of APs was detected in tested pairs.
source: In addition, NE released from LC/NE neurons may activate α2AR on adjacent LC/NE neurons or themselves to evoke hyperpolarization (Williams et al., 1985). However, no visible hyperpolarization in potential postsynaptic cells following single presynaptic APs or a train of APs was detected in these tested pairs as well, suggesting NE released from single LC neurons was not sufficient enough to activate the α2ARs.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from testing cell pairs.

claim: Sparse electrical connections were identified among LC/NE neurons at the adult stage.
source: With our multipatch recordings, we also examined electrical coupling between any cell pair and identified sparse electrical connections among LC/NE neurons at the adult stage (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on experimental testing shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 65 of the 1503 tested pairs across the inter-soma distance range of 16–531 µm were electrically coupled (4.3%).
source: According to this criterion, 65 of the 1503 tested pairs across the inter-soma distance range of 16–531 µm were electrically coupled (4.3%; Figure 3D, Figure 4F; also see below).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from testing 1503 cell pairs, shown in Figures 3D and 4F.

claim: The steady-state coupling coefficient averaged 0.040±0.028 (SD) (range: 0.0051–0.13; n=65).
source: For each coupled pair, the coupling coefficients were estimated and expressed as the average of the values in both directions. The steady-state coupling coefficient averaged 0.040±0.028 (SD) (range: 0.0051–0.13; n=65) (Figure 4D and I).
evidence: This is based on measurements from 65 electrically coupled pairs, shown in Figures 4D and 4I.

claim: The strength of electrical transmission in the vast majority of coupled pairs was bidirectional and symmetric.
source: The strength of electrical transmission in the vast majority of coupled pairs was bidirectional and symmetric (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: The conductance of putative gap junctions between LC/NE neurons was largely nonrectifying.
source: Estimates of the coupling coefficient in both directions for each pair showed a positive correlation with a slope of 1.03 (Figure 4D), not significantly different from 1 (p=0.8; Figure 4D), indicating that the conductance of putative gap junctions between LC/NE neurons was largely nonrectifying.
evidence: This is inferred from statistical analysis of coupling coefficients shown in Figure 4D.

claim: With an inter-soma distance <40 µm, the coupling rate between LC neurons was ~12%.
source: With an inter-soma distance <40 µm, the coupling rate between LC neurons was ~12%, indicating that electrical connections were prominent among LC neurons in adult mice.
evidence: This is based on analysis of coupling rate as a function of inter-soma distance.

claim: The coupling rate dropped quickly as the inter-soma distance increased from 40 µm.
source: However, the coupling rate dropped quickly as the inter-soma distance increased from 40 µm (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The coupling rate at young age (PND 13-21) was very similar to the rate found in adults (4.8%; 8 connections out of 165).
source: To examine whether this is the case, we performed additional multi-cell recordings of LC neurons from mice at the age of PND 13–21 (Figure 4F). Surprisingly, the coupling rate at this young age was very similar to the rate found in adults (4.8%; 8 connections out of 165, p>0.05, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from juvenile mice compared to adults, shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Of all FF–FF pairs, 8.7% were electrically coupled.
source: Of all FF–FF pairs (i.e., both cells are FF), we found 8.7% were electrically coupled (Figure 4G); of all MP–MP pairs (i.e., both cells are MP), 5.3% were electrically coupled (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of coupling rates by cell type, shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Of all MP–MP pairs, 5.3% were electrically coupled.
source: Of all FF–FF pairs (i.e., both cells are FF), we found 8.7% were electrically coupled (Figure 4G); of all MP–MP pairs (i.e., both cells are MP), 5.3% were electrically coupled (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of coupling rates by cell type, shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Only 0.8% of FF–MP pairs were electrically coupled.
source: By contrast, only 0.8% of FF–MP pairs were coupled (Figure 4G; p<0.0001 for both comparisons).
evidence: This is based on analysis of coupling rates by cell type, shown in Figure 4G.

claim: With the inter-soma distance of up to 40 µm, no connection was identified in FF–MP pairs (0 out of 55 tested pairs).
source: Interestingly, with the inter-soma distance of up to 40 µm, no connection was identified in FF–MP pairs (0 out of 55 tested pairs).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from testing 55 FF-MP pairs.

claim: The coupling rate for FF–FF pairs with inter-soma distance up to 40 µm was 31.4% (11 out of 35 tested pairs).
source: In contrast, the coupling rates for FF–FF and MP–MP pairs were much higher (11 out of 35 tested pairs, 31.4% for FF–FF, p<0.01 compared with FF–MP; 7 out of 65, 10.7% for MP–MP, p<0.01 compared with FF–MP; Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The coupling rate for MP–MP pairs with inter-soma distance up to 40 µm was 10.7% (7 out of 65 tested pairs).
source: In contrast, the coupling rates for FF–FF and MP–MP pairs were much higher (11 out of 35 tested pairs, 31.4% for FF–FF, p<0.01 compared with FF–MP; 7 out of 65, 10.7% for MP–MP, p<0.01 compared with FF–MP; Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Electrical connections in LC neurons generally form among cell pairs of the same cell type.
source: These results indicate that electrical connections in LC neurons generally form among cell pairs of the same cell type (Figures 3 and 4, Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 3, 4, 5, and 6.

claim: An FF is more likely to connect with another FF than an MP connects with another MP, particularly if the neurons are located nearby.
source: Within the same cell type, an FF is more likely to connect with another FF than an MP connects with another MP, particularly if the neurons are located nearby.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing coupling rates between FF-FF and MP-MP pairs at different inter-soma distances.

claim: Electrical coupling in FF–FF pairs had higher connection strength (i.e., higher coupling coefficients) than electrical coupling in MP–MP pairs.
source: In addition, electrical coupling in FF–FF pairs had higher connection strength (i.e., higher coupling coefficients) than electrical coupling in MP–MP pairs (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is based on comparison of coupling coefficients shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The vast majority of putative synapses were found to form between dendrites.
source: The vast majority of putative synapses were found to form between dendrites: this could be a single crossing point between two dendrites from a coupled pair (Figure 5C), or multiple merging sites between an entire dendrite from one cell and the entire dendrite from another cell (in parallel with each other along their course to the terminals; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of coupled pairs shown in Figures 5A and 5C.

claim: Only two coupled pairs (one FF–FF and one MP–MP) had putative synapses formed between the dendrite and the soma.
source: Only two coupled pairs (one FF–FF and one MP–MP) had putative synapses formed between the dendrite and the soma (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No putative synapses forming between two somata were identified in the data.
source: No putative synapses forming between two somata were identified in our data.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of all coupled pairs.

claim: There was no preferential synaptic location for either FF–FF coupled pairs or MP-MP coupled pairs.
source: Put together, our data suggest there was no preferential synaptic location for either FF–FF coupled pairs or MP-MP coupled pairs.
evidence: This is inferred from morphological analysis of putative synapses.

claim: The dendritic branches where the putative synapse was localized were generally first or second-order branches.
source: The dendritic branches where the putative synapse was localized were generally first or second-order branches and the putative synapses were most frequently located in the middle of the entire dendritic tree (average dendritic distance to soma: 155 µm, Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The putative synapses were most frequently located in the middle of the entire dendritic tree (average dendritic distance to soma: 155 µm).
source: The dendritic branches where the putative synapse was localized were generally first or second-order branches and the putative synapses were most frequently located in the middle of the entire dendritic tree (average dendritic distance to soma: 155 µm, Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on morphological measurements shown in Figure 5G.

claim: For each putative synapse, the dendric distance to one soma was linearly related to the distance to another soma with an r of 0.86.
source: For each putative synapse, the dendric distance to one soma was linearly related to the distance to another soma with an r of 0.86, indicating that the putative synapses sit a similar dendritic distance away from the two somata of the coupled pair (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Putative synaptic numbers and coupling coefficients showed a positive correlation (r=0.86).
source: Indeed, putative synaptic numbers and coupling coefficients showed a positive correlation (r=0.86, Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Electrical signals from one cell hardly pass to other cells via second-order coupling if they are not electrically coupled in the first order.
source: This indicates Cell 1 and Cell 8 both electrically connect with Cell 6, but Cell 1 and Cell 8 do not directly connect with each other. This result also indicates that electrical signals from one cell hardly pass to other cells via second-order coupling if they are not electrically coupled in the first order.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations of multicell recordings.

claim: 15 individual recording sets have more than two electrical connections (or electrically coupled pairs) identified.
source: Out of our all multiple-cell recording sets (≥3 cells), 15 individual recording sets have more than two electrical connections (or electrically coupled pairs) identified.
evidence: This is based on counting from the experimental dataset.

claim: One coupled pair often shared the same coupling partner with another coupled pair (i.e., A↔B↔C).
source: In these recording sets, one coupled pair often shared the same coupling partner with another coupled pair as illustrated in Figure 6A–C (i.e., A↔B↔C; each letter represents a cell; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figures 6A-C and 6D.

claim: Two coupled pairs without a sharing partner (i.e., A↔B, C↔D) were rare in the recording sets.
source: However, two coupled pairs without a sharing partner (i.e., A↔B, C↔D) were rare in our recording sets (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Electrically coupled cells tend to cluster together and form a chain-like pattern (i.e., A↔B↔C).
source: These data suggest each cell is not equally coupled with other cells in the network; instead, electrically coupled cells tend to cluster together and form a chain-like pattern (i.e., A↔B↔C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed patterns of electrical connections.

claim: The observed number of the chain-like connection pattern (n=16) was higher than the numbers predicted by the random connectivity model (n=12.9, 95% confidence interval [CI] = [6, 21]).
source: We found that the observed number of the chain-like connection pattern (n=16, Figure 6D) was higher than the numbers predicted by the random connectivity model (n=12.9, 95% confidence interval [CI] = [6, 21]), whereas the observed number of the non-chain-like patterns (n=5, Figure 6D) was significantly less than the numbers predicted by the model (n=11.6, 95% CI = [6, 19], p=0.01).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling comparing observed data to Model 1 predictions.

claim: The observed number of the non-chain-like patterns (n=5) was significantly less than the numbers predicted by the random connectivity model (n=11.6, 95% CI = [6, 19], p=0.01).
source: We found that the observed number of the chain-like connection pattern (n=16, Figure 6D) was higher than the numbers predicted by the random connectivity model (n=12.9, 95% confidence interval [CI] = [6, 21]), whereas the observed number of the non-chain-like patterns (n=5, Figure 6D) was significantly less than the numbers predicted by the model (n=11.6, 95% CI = [6, 19], p=0.01).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling comparing observed data to Model 1 predictions.

claim: The cluster index in the experimental dataset was 3.2, which was significantly higher than the number predicted by Model 1 (1.1, p=0.001).
source: We calculated the ratio of the chain-like pattern number to the non-chain-like pattern number to reflect the clustering degree of two electrical connections, which we henceforth called the cluster index (Figure 7A). The cluster index in our experimental dataset was 3.2, which was significantly higher than the number predicted by the model (1.1, p=0.001).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis comparing observed data to Model 1 predictions, shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The cell-type-specific connectivity rule cannot fully explain the dataset.
source: With this revised model (Model 2, see 'Materials and methods'), the observed numbers on average of the chain-like pattern again remained higher than the predicted numbers (n=12.6, 95% CI = [7, 18]), and the observed number of the non-chain-like pattern was still significantly lower than the numbers (n=11.2, 95% CI = [6,16], p<0.001) predicted by the model (Figure 7B). The cluster index predicted by Model 2 was very similar to that predicted by Model 1, and significantly lower than the observed index (Figure 7A), indicating that the cell-type-specific rule cannot explain our dataset.
evidence: This is inferred from statistical modeling comparing observed data to Model 2 predictions, shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Additional spatial connectivity rules could not explain the dataset.
source: The cluster index predicted by Model 3 was still significantly lower than the observed index (Figure 7A), indicating that additional spatial connectivity rules could not explain our dataset as well.
evidence: This is inferred from statistical modeling comparing observed data to Model 3 predictions, shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The clustering of two connections in the dataset (i.e., a chain-like pattern) cannot be explained by the random model and spatial and cell-type-specific rules.
source: In summary, the clustering of two connections in our dataset (i.e., a chain-like pattern) cannot be explained by the random model and spatial and cell-type-specific rules as shown above, suggesting an additional, possible chain-like rule dictating the organization of electrical connections in the LC network (note that all three models shared the assumption that the probability for two neurons to form an electrical connection is independent of all other pairwise connections, an assumption that the new rule will perhaps have to violate).
evidence: This is inferred from statistical modeling results comparing observed data to Models 1-3.

claim: The most frequent patterns of two electrical connections in the dataset are FF–FF–FF and MP–MP–MP.
source: Such an underlying new rule could impose on both cell types, and thus the most frequent patterns of two electrical connections in our dataset are FF–FF–FF and MP–MP–MP, while other combination patterns are either rare or not observed (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The most frequent pattern of three electrical connections was the chain-like pattern (A↔B↔C↔D).
source: Indeed, when we examined the organizing pattern of three electrical connections in those individual recording sets, the most frequent was still the chain-like pattern (A↔B↔C↔D, Figure 6D), while other possible organizing patterns including circular-like and hub cell-like patterns were rarely observed in our dataset (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Other possible organizing patterns including circular-like and hub cell-like patterns were rarely observed in the dataset.
source: Indeed, when we examined the organizing pattern of three electrical connections in those individual recording sets, the most frequent was still the chain-like pattern (A↔B↔C↔D, Figure 6D), while other possible organizing patterns including circular-like and hub cell-like patterns were rarely observed in our dataset (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The observed ratio of chain-like to non-chain-like patterns of triple connections was 2, significantly higher than the predicted ratio by Model 1 (0.68±0.25, p=0.001).
source: We again used the ratio of chain-like to non-chain-like patterns to measure the chain-like tendency in our dataset and compare it with model predictions. The observed ratio in our dataset was 2, significantly higher than the predicted ratio (0.68±0.25, p=0.001, Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling comparing observed data to Model 1 predictions, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In addition to spatial and cell-type-specific rule, an additional chain-like rule may apply for the organization of three electrical connections.
source: All simulations indicate that, in addition to spatial and cell-type-specific rule, an additional chain-like rule may apply for the organization of three electrical connections.
evidence: This is inferred from statistical modeling results for triple connections.

claim: This study may represent the first multicell patch recordings of a monoamine modulatory system in the brain.
source: In fact, this study may represent the first multicell patch recordings of a monoamine modulatory system in the brain, allowing for examining how monoaminergic neurons interact with each other at the single-cell level for the first time.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's methodology.

claim: Noradrenergic neurons in the LC could be classified into at least two major morpho-electric cell types.
source: Our results indicate noradrenergic neurons in the LC could be classified into at least two major morpho-electric cell types, and neurons within each cell type form a homotypic network module via gap junctions.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from morphological and electrophysiological characterization.

claim: Neurons within each cell type form a homotypic network module via gap junctions.
source: Our results indicate noradrenergic neurons in the LC could be classified into at least two major morpho-electric cell types, and neurons within each cell type form a homotypic network module via gap junctions.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing cell-type-specific electrical coupling.

claim: Each of these cell types may have preferential anatomical locations in LC and different projection targets.
source: Given that each of these cell types may have preferential anatomical locations in LC and different projection targets, each electrically coupled homotypic network may coordinate/synergize their input/output as a whole to engage in distinct functions of the circuits within its efferent domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed spatial distribution of cell types and supported by prior literature.

claim: Each electrically coupled homotypic network may coordinate/synergize their input/output as a whole to engage in distinct functions of the circuits within its efferent domain.
source: Given that each of these cell types may have preferential anatomical locations in LC and different projection targets, each electrically coupled homotypic network may coordinate/synergize their input/output as a whole to engage in distinct functions of the circuits within its efferent domain.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: The anterior horn of the LC and the ventral part of the LC core appears to be dominated by cells with a stellate multipolar soma.
source: The anterior horn of the LC and the ventral part of the LC core appears to be dominated by cells with a stellate multipolar soma, whereas its posterior horn and the dorsal edge of the LC core are dominated by cells with a fusiform-shaped soma (Loughlin et al., 1986; Swanson, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The posterior horn and the dorsal edge of the LC core are dominated by cells with a fusiform-shaped soma.
source: The anterior horn of the LC and the ventral part of the LC core appears to be dominated by cells with a stellate multipolar soma, whereas its posterior horn and the dorsal edge of the LC core are dominated by cells with a fusiform-shaped soma (Loughlin et al., 1986; Swanson, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LC neurons with distinct soma shapes preferentially project to different brain areas.
source: In addition, LC neurons with distinct soma shapes preferentially project to different brain areas (Loughlin et al., 1986; Waterhouse et al., 1983), warranting further exploration of the morphological diversity of LC neurons and their functional relevance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MPs had a longer AP with smaller amplitude than FFs.
source: While mature LC/NE neurons as a whole exhibit the stereotypical physiological properties that clearly differentiate them from hippocampal neurons, there are subtle differences between MP and FF in their individual APs: MPs had a longer AP with smaller amplitude than FFs.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements comparing MP and FF.

claim: FFs could sustain higher frequency firing than MPs with large suprathreshold depolarizing current injections.
source: Furthermore, FFs could sustain higher frequency firing than MPs with large suprathreshold depolarizing current injections.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements comparing MP and FF.

claim: FF may correspond to 'narrow' units identified during extracellular recordings of LC neurons, while MP may correspond to those 'wide' units.
source: The observation that FFs fire narrower spikes than MPs suggests FF may correspond to 'narrow' units identified during extracellular recordings of LC neurons, while MP may correspond to those 'wide' units (Su and Cohen, 2022; Totah et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on spike width comparisons and supported by citations.

claim: There is no consistent evidence supporting that FF cells correspond to those 'narrow' units, and MPs correspond to 'wild' units.
source: Therefore, there is no consistent evidence supporting that FF cells we defined here correspond to those 'narrow' units, and MPs correspond to 'wild' units.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the current findings with prior extracellular recording studies.

claim: Both single unit types may be from the same MP type reflecting within-MP functional heterogeneity.
source: Likely, each single unit type is not confined to a specific morphological type, or both single unit types may be from the same MP type reflecting within-MP functional heterogeneity. The latter may be more likely given that MPs are a predominant LC cell type and are more heterogeneous than FF in terms of soma size and spatial distribution (Loughlin et al., 1986), as well as electrophysiology properties including AP half-width (data not shown).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed heterogeneity of MPs and supported by citation.

claim: Fusiform-shaped cells in the posterior horn of the LC and the dorsal edge of the LC core preferentially project to the neocortex and hippocampus.
source: Indeed, previous studies indicate that fusiform-shaped cells in the posterior horn of the LC and the dorsal edge of the LC core preferentially project to the neocortex and hippocampus, while multipolar neurons in its anterior horn and/or the ventral part of the LC core preferentially project to the spinal cord, cerebellum, and hypothalamus (Loughlin et al., 1986; Waterhouse et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Multipolar neurons in the anterior horn and/or the ventral part of the LC core preferentially project to the spinal cord, cerebellum, and hypothalamus.
source: Indeed, previous studies indicate that fusiform-shaped cells in the posterior horn of the LC and the dorsal edge of the LC core preferentially project to the neocortex and hippocampus, while multipolar neurons in its anterior horn and/or the ventral part of the LC core preferentially project to the spinal cord, cerebellum, and hypothalamus (Loughlin et al., 1986; Waterhouse et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FF cells may correspond to those fusiform-shaped cells in the posterior horn of the LC and/or the dorsal edge of the LC core.
source: While it is difficult to register each cell in our slice recordings to their anatomical location in vivo, we reason that FF cells as we defined here correspond to those fusiform-shaped cells in the posterior horn of the LC and/or the dorsal edge of the LC core, while MP cells may correspond to those multipolar cells in the anterior horn and/or the ventral part of the core.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on morphological similarities.

claim: MP cells may correspond to those multipolar cells in the anterior horn and/or the ventral part of the core.
source: While it is difficult to register each cell in our slice recordings to their anatomical location in vivo, we reason that FF cells as we defined here correspond to those fusiform-shaped cells in the posterior horn of the LC and/or the dorsal edge of the LC core, while MP cells may correspond to those multipolar cells in the anterior horn and/or the ventral part of the core.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on morphological similarities.

claim: These two types may form separate LC subnetworks with distinct projection domains, each performing a nonoverlapping function in the brain.
source: If this is true, these two types as we defined here might form separate LC subnetworks with distinct projection domains, each performing a nonoverlapping function in the brain.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional organization of LC.

claim: Some LC neurons could express neuropeptide Y (NPY) and/or galanin.
source: Prior studies indicate some LC neurons could express neuropeptide Y (NPY) and/or galanin.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Neither NPY-expressing nor galanin-expressing LC neurons are confined to a specific morphological type.
source: However, it appears neither NPY-expressing nor galanin-expressing LC neurons are confined to a specific morphological type (Holets et al., 1988; Melander et al., 1986), suggesting that neither NPY nor galanin is a good candidate to differentiate the two LC morphological types.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Only a small subset of all terminals established by monoamine neurons may actually be specialized for the synaptic release of glutamate.
source: Nevertheless, we believe this type of connection, if it does exist, is sparse, given that only a small subset of all terminals established by monoamine neurons may actually be specialized for the synaptic release of glutamate (Trudeau, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A subset of noradrenergic axonal terminals may make glutamatergic synapses onto other target regions, including the spinal cord and the parabrachial nucleus neurons.
source: In addition, our result does not rule out the possibility that a subset of noradrenergic axonal terminals does make glutamatergic synapses onto other target regions, including the spinal cord and the parabrachial nucleus neurons (Fung et al., 1994a; Liu et al., 1995; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Alpha2 adrenoceptors (α2AR) are autoreceptors for NE which are expressed in the somata of LC/NE neurons.
source: Alpha2 adrenoceptors (α2AR) are such autoreceptors for NE which are expressed in the somata of LC/NE neurons as well.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about α2AR.

claim: NE released from individual LC/NE neurons is not sufficient to activate α2AR to evoke detectable inhibition on LC/NE neurons at least in the in vitro preparation.
source: After testing more than 1500 cell pairs, we did not find any detectable hyperpolarization following the stimulation of a single LC/NE neuron. While other unknown reasons may contribute to the absence of lateral inhibition, a plausible explanation is that NE released from individual LC/NE neurons is not sufficient to activate α2AR to evoke detectable inhibition on LC/NE neurons at least in our in vitro preparation.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations of testing more than 1500 cell pairs.

claim: α2AR-mediated lateral inhibition is a frequency-dependent population-wide phenomenon.
source: A recent study suggests that α2AR-mediated lateral inhibition is a frequency-dependent population-wide phenomenon, which can be readily detected when many neurons are simultaneously activated via an optogenetic approach (Davy et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: α2AR-mediated lateral inhibition appears to be a specific network interaction that is prevalent among LC neurons targeting distinct brain regions (module-specific), rather than a nonspecific, spatial 'surround' inhibition.
source: In addition, α2AR-mediated lateral inhibition appears to be a specific network interaction that is prevalent among LC neurons targeting distinct brain regions (module-specific), rather than a nonspecific, spatial 'surround' inhibition (Davy et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Several previous studies suggest that electrical coupling in the LC is negligible or absent in adult animals.
source: Several previous studies suggest that electrical coupling in the LC is negligible or absent in adult animals (Christie and Jelinek, 1993; Christie et al., 1989; Travagli et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The multicell recordings provide a direct demonstration of electrical coupling established by mature LC/NE neurons with a coupling rate consistent with a previous report from extracellular recording.
source: In contrast to these studies, our multicell recordings provide a direct demonstration of electrical coupling established by mature LC/NE neurons with a coupling rate consistent with a previous report from extracellular recording (Totah et al., 2018), substantiating prior evidence that electrical coupling is still an important mechanism for LC/NE neurons to interact with each other in adult animals (Alvarez et al., 2002; Rash et al., 2007; Van Bockstaele et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: An electrical coupling rate ranging from 15% to 80% has been reported in many brain regions based on pairwise testing of narrowly spaced cells of the same cell type from juvenile animals.
source: An electrical coupling rate ranging from 15% to 80% has been reported in many brain regions based on pairwise testing of narrowly spaced cells of the same cell type from juvenile animals (Curti et al., 2012; Devor and Yarom, 2002; Long et al., 2004; Tamás et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several studies indicate the electrical coupling rate often drops to zero once the inter-soma distance increases to more than 40 µm.
source: Indeed, several studies indicate the electrical coupling rate often drops to zero once the inter-soma distance increases to more than 40 µm (Beierlein et al., 2000; Curti et al., 2012; Galarreta and Hestrin, 2001; Galarreta and Hestrin, 2002; Gibson et al., 1999; Tamás et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Electrical coupling appears to decrease with age in most brain structures.
source: In addition, electrical coupling appears to decrease with age in most brain structures (Peinado et al., 1993), including in LC (Christie and Jelinek, 1993; Christie et al., 1989; Travagli et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A direct comparison of the coupling rate in adults to juvenile animals did not reveal a significant difference between the two ages.
source: However, a direct comparison of the coupling rate in adults to juvenile animals did not reveal a significant difference between the two ages, indicating that electrical coupling in the LC may be less subject to developmental change than previously thought.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing adult and juvenile mice.

claim: Gap junctions generally form between cell pairs of the same type (homotypic gap junctions), while gap junctions between different cell types (heterotypic gap junctions) are rare or absent in most brain regions.
source: It is well documented that gap junctions generally form between cell pairs of the same type (homotypic gap junctions), while gap junctions between different cell types (heterotypic gap junctions) are rare or absent in most brain regions (Peinado et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Each LC neuron is intricately connected with their very close neighboring neurons of the same type to constitute cell-type-specific electrical subnetworks (FF subnetwork vs. MP subnetwork).
source: The result suggests that each LC neuron is intricately connected with their very close neighboring neurons of the same type to constitute cell-type-specific electrical subnetworks (FF subnetwork vs. MP subnetwork), each of which may synchronize independently via extensive gap junctions.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data on cell-type-specific electrical coupling.

claim: This finding provides a plausible cellular mechanism for prior observations that LC pairwise correlated firing and LC ensembles identified in extracellular recordings are cell-type specific.
source: This finding provides a plausible cellular mechanism for prior observations that LC pairwise correlated firing and LC ensembles identified in extracellular recordings are cell-type specific (Noei et al., 2022; Totah et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior observations, supported by citations.

claim: The coupling rate between FF–FF pairs is more than threefold higher than that between MP-MP pairs.
source: Of note, the coupling rate between FF–FF pairs is more than threefold higher than that between MP-MP pairs, suggesting that the MP electrical subnetwork may be smaller in terms of cell population than the FF subnetwork.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing coupling rates.

claim: A lower coupling rate among MPs may suggest that MPs are more heterogeneous than FFs.
source: Alternatively, a lower coupling rate among MPs may suggest that MPs are more heterogeneous than FFs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about MP heterogeneity.

claim: MP cells in each LC subregion may only electrically connect with MP cells in the same LC subregion to form subregion-specific MP subnetworks, each of which performs unique functions.
source: Therefore, MP cells in each LC subregion may only electrically connect with MP cells in the same LC subregion to form subregion-specific MP subnetworks, each of whicht performs unique functions (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about MP subnetwork organization, illustrated in Figure 7C.

claim: Close appositions between two neurons identified under the light microscope could be reliably confirmed as real electrical synapses by follow-up electron microscope studies.
source: While close appositions between two neurons do not necessarily mean electrical synapses, such contact sites identified under the light microscope could be reliably confirmed as real electrical synapses by follow-up electron microscope studies (Fukuda and Kosaka, 2000; Fukuda and Kosaka, 2003; Tamás et al., 2000; Vervaeke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: More than 50% of electrically coupled pairs have only one putative synapse.
source: Our examination of close appositions between electrically coupled pairs indicates more than 50% of electrically coupled pairs have only one putative synapse, and multiple contact sites between pairs are less frequent.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of coupled pairs.

claim: Almost all putative synapses were found to occur between dendrites, corroborating a previous LC study in rats.
source: Almost all putative synapses were found to occur between dendrites, corroborating a previous LC study in rats (Ishimatsu and Williams, 1996).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis and supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Dendro-dendritic synapses appear to be a dominant form of electrical synapses across brain regions.
source: In fact, dendro-dendritic synapses appear to be a dominant form of electrical synapses across brain regions (Fukuda and Kosaka, 2000; Fukuda and Kosaka, 2003; Hidaka et al., 2004; Sotelo et al., 1974; Vervaeke et al., 2010; Waterhouse et al., 1983), while somato-dendritic or somato-somatic ones are much less common (Curti et al., 2012; Tamás et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Electrical synapses in dendrites are localized further away from the soma as animals get older.
source: In addition, electrical synapses in dendrites are localized further away from the soma as animals get older (Fukuda and Kosaka, 2000; Fukuda and Kosaka, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gap junctions found at distal dendritic sites can interact locally with chemical synaptic inputs to drive synchronized spiking.
source: Recent work has shown those gap junctions found at distal dendritic sites can interact locally with chemical synaptic inputs to drive synchronized spiking. While coupled potentials are small at the soma, these electrical signals are expected to be larger near gap junctions, where they enable excitatory synaptic charge to spread into the dendrites of neighboring coupled neurons (Vervaeke et al., 2012), and/or sum with chemical synaptic inputs to generate dendritic spikes that actively propagate with little delay to the soma and drive action potentials with high fidelity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Gap junctions may promote the synchronized response of an electrically coupled neuronal population to certain specific synaptic inputs.
source: The former may promote the synchronized response of an electrically coupled neuronal population to certain specific synaptic inputs, while the latter allows weak distal gap junction inputs to synchronize somatic action potentials, promoting synchronized spiking of electrically coupled neurons upon common chemical synaptic input (Migliore et al., 2005; Schoppa and Westbrook, 2002; Trenholm et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gap junctions allow weak distal gap junction inputs to synchronize somatic action potentials, promoting synchronized spiking of electrically coupled neurons upon common chemical synaptic input.
source: The former may promote the synchronized response of an electrically coupled neuronal population to certain specific synaptic inputs, while the latter allows weak distal gap junction inputs to synchronize somatic action potentials, promoting synchronized spiking of electrically coupled neurons upon common chemical synaptic input (Migliore et al., 2005; Schoppa and Westbrook, 2002; Trenholm et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gap junction studies with the dye-coupling approach may provide an insight into network organization questions.
source: Gap junction studies with the dye-coupling approach may provide an insight into these questions (Curti et al., 2012; Long et al., 2004), but the neuron clusters labeled by this approach could result from a second-order coupling, in addition to first-order coupling – these couplings are not otherwise discriminable – greatly compounding interpretation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Somatic membrane potentials in a pre-junctional cell are likely to be highly attenuated by the time they reach a post-junctional cell given gap junctions being located at the dendrite far away from the soma.
source: First, given gap junctions being located at the dendrite far away from the soma, somatic membrane potentials in a pre-junctional cell are likely to be highly attenuated by the time they reach a post-junctional cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the morphological location of gap junctions.

claim: Gap junctions with a dominant dendrodendritic form identified with pairwise recordings should be essentially first-order gap junctions.
source: It is reasonable to conclude that such highly attenuated coupled potential from the first-order coupling can hardly propagate any further into cells through second-order coupling. Thus, the gap junctions with a dominant dendrodendritic form identified with pairwise recordings should be essentially first-order gap junctions, but this assertion has never been directly confirmed as yet.
evidence: This is inferred from the expected attenuation of signals through dendrodendritic gap junctions.

claim: The multicell recording sets allowed for directly testing the assertion that gap junctions identified with pairwise patch recordings in LC are first-order and ruled out the possibility of second-order coupling.
source: Our multicell recording sets allowed for directly testing said assertion and ruled out the possibility that gap junctions identified with pairwise patch recordings in LC could result from a second-order coupling.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from multicell recordings.

claim: A chain-like pattern of two connections (A↔B↔C) is overrepresented in the dataset.
source: With the support from the simulation with a random connectivity model, a chain-like pattern of two connections (A↔B↔C) is overrepresented in our dataset.
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling comparing observed data to random connectivity predictions.

claim: Revising the model by adding spatial and cell-type-specific connectivity rules did not significantly improve simulation results.
source: However, revising our model by adding these connectivity rules did not significantly improve simulation results, and a chain-like pattern of two connections (A↔B↔C) remains unexplained.
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling results.

claim: In addition to spatial and cell-type-specific rules governing LC electrical connections, there is an additional chain-like connectivity rule.
source: All simulations suggest that, in addition to spatial and cell-type-specific rules governing LC electrical connections, there is an additional chain-like connectivity rule that may contribute to the overrepresentation of a chain-like pattern of two connections in our dataset.
evidence: This is inferred from statistical modeling results.

claim: The chain-like connectivity rule may be a general wiring principle dictating a whole electrically coupled network composed of hundreds of neurons.
source: While we could not test if this additional connectivity rule may apply to four or more connections for now (no four connections were found in our dataset), the chain-like connectivity rule may be a general wiring principle dictating a whole electrically coupled network composed of hundreds of neurons (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about network organization, illustrated in Figure 7C.

claim: Previous dye-based studies suggest the same chain-like connectivity rule in many brain regions and cell types, including LC.
source: Indeed, previous dye-based studies suggest the same connectivity rule in many brain regions and cell types, including LC (Christie and Jelinek, 1993; Curti et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2014; Long et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: If a chain-like organizing pattern is true, then the dye injection of a single cell can only label the maximum of two additional cells if only first-order coupled cells are labeled.
source: If a chain-like organizing pattern is true, then the dye injection of a single cell can only label the maximum of two additional cells if only first-order coupled cells are labeled.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the chain-like connectivity hypothesis.

claim: The cluster of labeled cells in dye-based studies is often small with a maximum of two additional labeled cells.
source: Indeed, the cluster of labeled cells in these studies is often small with a maximum of two additional labeled cells (Christie and Jelinek, 1993; Curti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gap junctions between five neurons in the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus have been shown to arrange like a chain-like pattern across neurons.
source: The most convincing evidence for this rule comes from the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus, where gap junctions between five neurons have been elegantly shown to arrange like a chain-like pattern across neurons (Curti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.
